items.title: L14: When a manager hints at the outcome
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: Managers sometimes say things that sound like promises: you are the obvious person for this, the job is yours if you apply, or we will make sure it works out. Such remarks may be well meant, but they sit uneasily with fair and open competition. A manager may legitimately encourage someone to apply, give feedback on readiness and share what the role involves. A manager may not pre-select a candidate, promise an outcome, tailor the advert to a named person, or pass confidential information about the competition to one candidate. If you are on the receiving end, treat any hint as non-binding: you still have to compete and you will be assessed against the same criteria as everyone else. Do not stop preparing or ease off your evidence, and do not tell colleagues you have been promised the job. If the hint concerns you, because it suggests the outcome is decided, you can raise it quietly with HR or the nominated officer without making accusations, describing what was said and when. If you are the manager, avoid language that could be taken as a commitment, and if you are on the panel or have influence over it, declare your relationship and step back. Advertising a post with criteria that match only one person, or setting an unusually short closing date, can also undermine openness. The Civil Service Code requires objectivity and impartiality, which means taking decisions on merit and evidence and not on personal preference or convenience. Departments that find pre-selection may have to re-run a competition, and the Commission may examine a breach of the Principles.

questions.prompt: A manager tells you the job is yours if you apply. How should you treat this?

options.text: As non-binding, since you must still compete on the same criteria
As a signal to reduce your preparation, since the outcome is settled
As something to tell colleagues so that they do not waste time applying
As a commitment that you can rely on, since managers know the post best

questions.hint: A hint cannot replace a fair competition.

questions.prompt: Which manager behaviour is legitimate?

options.text: Writing criteria that only one named person could meet
Encouraging a member of staff to apply and giving honest feedback on readiness
Sharing the list of other applicants with a favoured candidate
Promising a candidate a particular result if they choose to apply

questions.hint: Encouragement is fine, pre-selection is not.

questions.prompt: Which practice would indicate possible pre-selection?

options.text: An advert open to the usual pool for a normal period of time
An advert that lists clear criteria relevant to the work of the post
An advert with criteria that match only one named person
An advert that names a contact for reasonable adjustments

questions.prompt: You are worried a hint means the outcome is decided. What is a measured response?

options.text: Ask the other candidates to withdraw so that the process is cleaner
Accuse the manager openly at the next team meeting so that others hear
Withdraw from the competition without comment to avoid any conflict
Raise it quietly with HR or the nominated officer, describing what was said and when

questions.prompt: Why does an unusually short closing date raise concern?

options.text: It can limit the number of people who learn of the vacancy, undermining openness
The panel will have too little time to read and score each application
It breaches the rules on the number of stages that a competition may use
Internal candidates are automatically favoured whenever the date is short

questions.hint: Openness depends on a reasonable chance to apply.

questions.prompt: Which Civil Service Code values are most engaged by pre-selection?

options.text: Speed and efficiency in filling the post once it falls vacant
Integrity and respect for the minister who leads the department
Honesty and loyalty to colleagues who have worked with you for years
Objectivity and impartiality

questions.hint: Decisions must be on merit and evidence.

questions.prompt: A manager on the panel has promised a candidate the job. What should the manager do?

options.text: Ask the candidate to keep the promise confidential until the interview
Wait for the interview to see whether the candidate performs well enough
Declare the relationship, step back and avoid any commitment in future
Stay on the panel but score the candidate generously to honour the promise

questions.hint: A manager with a commitment should step back.

questions.prompt: What may happen if a department finds that a candidate was pre-selected?

options.text: The post is automatically offered to whoever was placed second
It may have to re-run the competition and the Commission may examine a breach
The candidate's appointment is confirmed once the manager has apologised
The panel's scores are averaged with the manager's own view of the candidate

questions.prompt: Is it appropriate to tell colleagues that you have been promised the job?

options.text: It is not, since you have not been appointed and may mislead or upset them
It is appropriate, because it helps colleagues plan their own applications
It is appropriate provided your manager has agreed to your telling them
It is appropriate when the post is open only to internal candidates

questions.hint: Do not spread a promise that may be invalid.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures why hints matter?

options.text: They are a normal part of recruitment and carry no risk at all
They are criminal offences in every case, whatever the intention
They are always deliberate attempts to defraud the department of a post
They can compromise fair and open competition even when well meant

questions.hint: Intent does not remove the effect on fairness.

items.title: L14: Calibrating and moderating sift scores
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: When several people score a large number of applications, differences in standards creep in. One scorer may be generous, another strict, a third prone to marking up the first few applications they read. To reduce this, departments use calibration and moderation. Before scoring starts, the scorers read the criteria and the scoring guide and look at sample applications together, agreeing what a score of, say, a mid-range mark looks like in evidence. They then score independently and compare, discussing any large differences. During scoring a lead scorer may sample marked papers to check consistency. After scoring, moderation looks at the distribution of marks, at borderline cases around the pass mark and at any anomalies, such as a scorer whose average is far from the rest. If differences are not explained by the evidence, the scores are adjusted or the application is re-scored. A second scorer is often used for borderline applications. Records of moderation decisions should be kept, with the reason for each change. This process protects candidates from the luck of which scorer they drew. It is not a way to adjust scores toward a preferred outcome: scores should change only because of the evidence in the application and the scoring guide. Names and personal details are often removed before scoring, to reduce bias, though this can be difficult where examples are specific to a department. As a candidate, the lesson is that evidence should be clear to a reader who knows nothing of your team.

questions.prompt: Why do departments calibrate scorers before scoring begins?

options.text: To give each scorer a quota of high marks they are allowed to award
To agree what a given score looks like in evidence so that standards are consistent
To let scorers see each other's final decisions before they begin
To decide in advance which candidates are expected to pass the sift

questions.prompt: What typically happens during moderation?

options.text: Candidates are asked to rewrite their statements to meet the standard
The most senior scorer's marks replace those of the other scorers
Marks distributions, borderline cases and anomalies are reviewed
An average mark is added to every application to even out differences

questions.prompt: A scorer's average is far from the rest. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Remove that scorer's marks without discussing them with anyone
Ask the scorer to raise their marks so that they match the others
Check whether the evidence explains the difference and re-score if it does not
Average that scorer's marks with those of the remaining scorers

questions.hint: Differences should be tested against evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is a second scorer often used for borderline applications?

options.text: A second scorer is required for every application in every competition
A small difference in marks can decide whether someone progresses
Borderline applications are always the strongest in the whole field
Borderline applications cannot lawfully be scored by only one person

questions.hint: Borderline cases are where fairness matters most.

questions.prompt: Which statement about changing scores in moderation is correct?

options.text: Scores should change only because of the evidence and the scoring guide
Scores can be changed to fill a fixed number of interview places
Scores can be changed to favour internal candidates over external ones
Scores can be changed to reach a preferred ranking among the candidates

questions.hint: Moderation is not a route to a desired outcome.

questions.prompt: Why are names and personal details often removed before scoring?

options.text: To protect candidates' names from being published after the competition
To stop scorers from knowing the grade of the candidate they are scoring
To speed up the process and reduce the time that scoring takes
To reduce the risk of conscious or unconscious bias

questions.prompt: Why can anonymisation be difficult in internal competitions?

options.text: Names are required to be included in every sift answer by the system
Examples may be so specific to a department that the writer can be identified
Internal candidates normally refuse to have their applications anonymised
The Commission prohibits anonymisation of internal competitions entirely

questions.prompt: Why should moderation decisions be recorded with reasons?

options.text: To fill the quality report that the department sends to its minister
To allow scores to be altered later without anyone being told
To provide material for each candidate's personal file in the department
To show that changes were made on the evidence and to support feedback and complaints

questions.prompt: What lesson can a candidate draw about writing evidence?

options.text: Use departmental jargon freely so that scorers see that you belong
Keep answers short so that scorers can fill the gaps themselves
Make it clear to a reader who knows nothing of your team
Assume that the scorer already knows your manager's view of your work

questions.hint: Scorers read many statements and need clarity.

questions.prompt: A lead scorer samples marked applications during scoring. What is the purpose?

options.text: To check consistency across scorers before it becomes a problem
To mark down scorers who give higher marks than their colleagues
To shorten the process by allowing later stages to be skipped
To choose which candidates will be invited to interview directly

items.title: L14: Defending a panel decision and giving honest feedback
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: Panels sometimes face challenge after a decision, from candidates, managers or colleagues. The best defence is a good process: published criteria, consistent questions, independent scoring, notes written at the time and a clear link between the evidence and each score. When feedback is requested, the panel should be able to say what each score reflected, what would have scored higher and how the candidate compared with the standard, without comparing named individuals. Feedback must be honest and constructive. It should not hide weaknesses behind vague phrases such as you were very close, if the gap was in fact large, and it should not promise outcomes in future. Nor should feedback reveal other candidates' scores or personal information. A panel member should not give informal feedback separately from the agreed account, because inconsistent messages can look like unfairness. Where there are concerns that the decision was affected by bias or a breach of the Principles, the panel should be open to review rather than defensive. If the review finds an error, the department should correct it, which could mean re-scoring or re-running a competition, and the panel should learn from it. If a candidate disagrees with the outcome but the process was fair, the decision stands, and the panel can explain that the candidate may use the complaints process if they believe the Principles were breached. Treat challenges as a chance to show that the process is sound, and be polite in every conversation.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest defence of a panel decision?

options.text: A sound process with criteria, consistent questions, independent scoring and notes
A statement that the decision is final and cannot be discussed
The collective years of experience that the panel members have
The seniority of the panel chair, whose judgement is rarely questioned

questions.prompt: Which feedback best serves an unsuccessful candidate?

options.text: A list of the other candidates' scores so that they can compare
A clear account of what each score reflected and what would have scored higher
A promise that they will succeed if they apply again next time
A general remark that they were very close to being appointed

questions.hint: Feedback should be honest and specific.

questions.prompt: A panel member wants to give extra informal feedback that differs from the agreed account. What is the risk?

options.text: It is prohibited by criminal law in every recruitment process
It will change the candidate's score once the feedback has been given
Inconsistent messages can look like unfairness and confuse the candidate
It will be added to the candidate's record on the department's system

questions.prompt: Why is saying you were very close misleading if the gap was large?

options.text: It reveals the other candidate's score to the unsuccessful person
It proves that the panel was biased in the way it assessed
It breaches the confidentiality rules that apply to panel members
It hides weaknesses and gives the candidate a false basis for future applications

questions.prompt: Should feedback reveal other candidates' scores?

options.text: It should if the candidate asks for it in writing
It should, because it shows how the final ranking was reached
It should not, since that discloses personal information
It should if the other candidate is also an internal applicant

questions.prompt: A concern is raised that bias affected a decision. What is the proper attitude?

options.text: Replace the whole panel immediately without any review of the facts
Ignore the concern as unfounded unless a formal complaint is made
Defend the decision strongly to protect the reputation of the panel
Be open to review rather than defensive

questions.prompt: A review finds a scoring error that affected the outcome. What should the department do?

options.text: Offer the unsuccessful candidate a different post instead
Correct it, which could mean re-scoring or re-running the competition
Leave it as it is, because the outcome has already been announced
Remove the records of the competition so that no one can see the error

questions.prompt: The process was fair but a candidate disagrees with the outcome. What is correct?

options.text: The decision stands, with the complaints process open if the Principles were breached
The decision is reversed so that the candidate is content with the result
The panel must repeat the interview with a new chair
The candidate may choose the successful person from those shortlisted

questions.hint: Disagreement alone is not a breach.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is an example of unhelpful feedback?

options.text: You gave good answers, so don't worry about anything
Your example showed your role but not the result it achieved
The evidence for the third criterion was thin and general
Your answer to the second question lacked a clear outcome

questions.prompt: How should panels treat challenges after a decision?

options.text: As an opportunity to defend the preferred candidate more firmly
As a chance to show the process is sound and be polite throughout
As an annoyance that should be left unanswered until it passes
As a threat that should be handled only by the most senior panel member

items.title: L14: From colleague to manager after promotion
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Behaviours
items.body: A promotion within your own team changes your relationships overnight, and how you manage the first months affects your reputation and your next move. The people who were peers are now your reports, some of whom may have applied for the same post. Start by talking to each of them individually, listening before announcing changes, and acknowledging that the shift may feel awkward. Be clear about your role and expectations, without pretending that the past relationships did not exist. Avoid favouring former friends or distancing yourself abruptly. Treat candidates who were unsuccessful with particular care: they may be disappointed, and a fair, open conversation about their development can retain their goodwill and talent. Establish routines, such as regular one-to-ones, objectives and feedback, and do not make big changes immediately unless there is a pressing reason. Seek early advice from your own manager and a mentor on areas you have not led before, such as performance conversations, sickness absence or handling a conflict. Take the line manager training your department offers, and learn the HR processes you will be expected to use. Probation or a settling-in period often applies to promotions, so check what is expected and ask for feedback at intervals. Keep boundaries around confidentiality: you may now hold information that you cannot share with former peers. Document your achievements from the start, since evidence from your first months at the new grade will build the case for your next step.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible first step on becoming manager of former peers?

options.text: Announce a list of changes at the first team meeting to set direction
Ask colleagues to treat you exactly as they did before promotion
Talk to each person individually and listen before announcing changes
Avoid your former peers for a while so that you appear impartial

questions.hint: Start by listening and acknowledging the shift.

questions.prompt: How should you treat colleagues who applied for the same post and were unsuccessful?

options.text: By suggesting that they move to another team to avoid friction
By giving them the least demanding tasks to avoid disappointing them
By avoiding the subject altogether so that no one feels uncomfortable
With particular care, offering an honest conversation about their development

questions.prompt: Which of these is a risk of favouring former friends in the team?

options.text: It will lower your pay at the end of the following year
It will cancel your probation period automatically
It is a breach of the Official Secrets Act in some departments
It can look unfair and damage your standing with the rest of the team

questions.prompt: Why avoid sweeping changes in the first weeks?

options.text: You need to understand the team first, unless there is a pressing reason
Changes are valid only once the team has voted on them
New managers are not allowed to change anything during probation
Any change must be approved first by the Civil Service Commission

questions.prompt: Who is a good source of early advice on unfamiliar areas such as performance conversations?

options.text: Generic advice from internet searches about managing former peers
A colleague in another department with no knowledge of your team
Your own manager and a mentor
Your direct reports, since they know the team's work best

questions.prompt: What should you check about probation after a promotion?

options.text: Whether probation applies to the members of your new team
What is expected and how and when feedback will be given
Whether probation will last for the rest of your career in the grade
Whether probation can be waived by your own manager if you ask

questions.prompt: Which boundary is important after promotion?

options.text: Sharing everything with your former peers to maintain trust and openness
Keeping confidential the information you now hold that you cannot share with former peers
Refusing to attend peer meetings that you used to attend
Keeping your own pay secret from your manager so that you appear modest

questions.prompt: What is a sound routine to establish early?

options.text: Occasional meetings called when a problem arises in the team
A weekly social event to keep morale high
Regular one-to-ones with objectives and feedback
Annual reviews only, to avoid over-managing the team

questions.prompt: Why document achievements from the start of the new grade?

options.text: They replace the need for any formal appraisal in the first year
They reduce your workload by letting others see what you have done
They must be submitted to HR at the end of probation by rule
They build evidence for your next step

questions.hint: Evidence at the new grade is persuasive.

questions.prompt: How should you treat the awkwardness of the shift?

options.text: Acknowledge it openly rather than pretending the past relationships did not exist
Ignore it until someone raises the issue directly with you
Deny that anything has changed so that people are not unsettled
Ask your manager to announce that the matter will not be discussed

items.title: L14: Part-time, flexible working and promotion fairness
items.source: Equality Act 2010; Civil Service Recruitment Principles; ACAS guidance
items.body: People who work part time or flexibly, who are often women or carers, can be disadvantaged in promotion if processes assume full-time presence. This can raise indirect discrimination, which occurs when a provision, criterion or practice applies to everyone but puts people with a protected characteristic at a particular disadvantage, and the employer cannot show it is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. For example, a rule that a promoted post must be held full time may exclude many people who work part time, so the department should ask whether the post could be done in a job share or on reduced hours, and whether the requirement is truly needed. Under the Part-time Workers regulations, part-time workers should not be treated less favourably than comparable full-time workers without objective justification. Employees can make a statutory request for flexible working, which the employer must consider reasonably and respond to within the required period, and can refuse only on specified business grounds. A manager should not assume that a part-time worker is less committed or unavailable for development, and should offer stretch work and talent opportunities on the same basis. If you work part time and want to progress, check whether the advert mentions flexible working, ask about job share possibilities and ask how the post could be configured. Evidence is judged on quality, not on hours worked: a part-time person can show leadership, outcomes and impact. If you believe you have been treated unfairly, use the grievance procedure and take advice early, as there are time limits for legal claims.

questions.prompt: What is indirect discrimination?

options.text: A neutral rule that disadvantages a protected group and cannot be justified
A rule that is applied to only one named person in the team
A comment about a person's characteristics made in an interview
A decision made deliberately because of a person's protected characteristic

questions.hint: Indirect discrimination is about neutral rules with unequal effect.

questions.prompt: A rule requires a promoted post to be held full time. What should the department ask?

options.text: Whether part-time staff should be asked to move to full time before applying
Whether the requirement is truly needed and whether a job share or reduced hours would work
Whether the requirement can be kept confidential from applicants
Whether the post should be moved to a different department

questions.hint: The department must justify the requirement.

questions.prompt: Which principle applies to part-time workers?

options.text: They must be offered promoted posts before full-time colleagues
They cannot apply for promotion unless they move to full time
They must not be treated less favourably without objective justification
They are entitled to the same hours as comparable full-time workers

questions.prompt: What can an employee do about working pattern under the flexible working rules?

options.text: Ask only after completing one year in the post
Require the employer to accept the request whatever the circumstances
Choose any working pattern without the employer's agreement
Make a statutory request that the employer must consider reasonably

questions.hint: The right is to request and have it considered.

questions.prompt: On what basis can an employer refuse a flexible working request?

options.text: Only on specified business grounds
Because the work of the team is generally important
On any ground that the manager personally prefers at the time
Because the employee is at a junior grade in the team

questions.hint: Refusal must fall within the statutory grounds.

questions.prompt: Which assumption should a manager avoid?

options.text: That a part-time worker should be offered stretch work as well
That a part-time worker can show leadership and impact in the role
That a part-time worker may have different availability for meetings
That a part-time worker is less committed or unavailable for development

questions.hint: Do not assume lack of commitment.

questions.prompt: How is evidence of leadership judged?

options.text: On length of service in the department rather than the example itself
On quality and impact rather than hours worked
On whether the person is in the office every day of the week
On the number of hours worked in the week during the example

questions.prompt: You work part time and want to progress. What is a sensible step?

options.text: Hide your working pattern from the panel so that it is not considered
Assume that part-time staff cannot apply for senior posts at all
Check whether the advert mentions flexible working and ask about job share
Move to full time until you are promoted and then change back

questions.prompt: Where should you begin if you believe you have been treated unfairly?

options.text: Use the grievance procedure and take advice early, because time limits apply
Wait until the end of the year to see if things change by themselves
Post about it publicly so that the department responds quickly
Resign immediately so that you can look for a fairer employer

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of indirect discrimination risk in promotion?

options.text: A requirement to meet the stated criteria for the post
An unnecessary full-time requirement that excludes part-timers
A requirement to attend interview at a set time and place
A requirement to hold a qualification that the post genuinely needs

questions.hint: Unjustified rules with unequal effect are the risk.

items.title: L14: Mentoring, sponsorship and fair access to opportunity
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; departmental talent guidance
items.body: Informal networks can speed careers, but they also create unequal access. A mentor gives advice and perspective and does not need to be in your reporting line. A sponsor is typically more senior and uses their influence to advocate for you, recommend you for stretch assignments and speak for you in rooms you are not in. Both can help, but they are different and a sponsor's help is the more powerful and the more delicate. A sponsor may recommend you to take on a high-profile project, and that is legitimate; a sponsor cannot decide a competition in your favour or give you access to information that other candidates do not have. Where opportunities such as acting up, loans, stretch tasks and talent schemes are allocated informally, those who are less visible, work part time, are newly arrived or lack networks can lose out. Departments therefore use transparent processes: advertising opportunities, expression of interest routes, rotation and criteria. If you are a manager, be aware of the opportunities you can give, and offer them widely, with fair criteria. If you are seeking a sponsor, do not rely on chance: make your work visible, ask for feedback, volunteer for cross-team work and approach potential sponsors with a specific request. Be careful that a relationship does not become a conflict of interest if the sponsor sits on a panel for a post you are applying for; declare it. Many departments run formal mentoring schemes and reverse mentoring, and some professions have sponsorship programmes for under-represented groups.

questions.prompt: What best distinguishes a sponsor from a mentor?

options.text: A sponsor is always your line manager, while a mentor is outside it
A sponsor is paid by the department, while a mentor is a volunteer
A sponsor is more senior and advocates for you, a mentor advises
A mentor decides your promotions, while a sponsor only gives advice

questions.prompt: Which sponsor action is legitimate?

options.text: Sharing the interview questions with you in advance
Adjusting your score on the panel by a mark or two
Deciding the outcome of a competition in your favour
Recommending you for a high-profile stretch assignment

questions.prompt: Why can informal allocation of opportunities disadvantage some staff?

options.text: It is unlawful in every circumstance and must be stopped
People who are less visible, part time or newly arrived can miss out
It is faster, so more people benefit from the opportunities
Informal allocation always favours women over men in the team

questions.hint: Informal routes advantage the well connected.

questions.prompt: How do departments reduce unequal access to opportunities?

options.text: By letting each manager decide privately who should be offered them
By removing stretch opportunities altogether so that no one benefits
By advertising opportunities and using clear criteria
By giving opportunities to the longest-serving staff first

questions.prompt: What should a manager who holds opportunities to give do?

options.text: Offer them widely with fair criteria
Allocate them by seniority so that no one can object
Give them to the people they trust most, who are likely to perform
Keep them for a future promotion board to allocate

questions.prompt: Which approach to finding a sponsor is most effective?

options.text: Ask the most senior person you know to sponsor you at your first meeting
Ask your line manager to choose a sponsor on your behalf
Wait for a sponsor to notice your work without any action on your part
Make your work visible and approach potential sponsors with a specific request

questions.prompt: A sponsor sits on the panel for a post you apply for. What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing, in case declaring it harms your chances
Ask the sponsor to give you a higher score than others
Withdraw from the competition without asking the chair
Declare the relationship so the panel can manage the conflict

questions.prompt: Which statement about mentoring is correct?

options.text: A mentor must be at a lower grade than the mentee
A mentor must be your line manager so that they know your work
A mentor need not be in your reporting line
A mentor decides your appraisal marking at the end of the year

questions.hint: Mentors can be anyone with experience.

questions.prompt: What is reverse mentoring?

options.text: A junior colleague mentors a senior one on fresh perspectives
A mentoring arrangement that is cancelled by the mentee
A senior colleague mentors a junior colleague for a set period
A mentor swaps roles with the mentee for a few weeks

questions.hint: Reverse mentoring flips the usual direction.

questions.prompt: Why do some professions run sponsorship programmes for under-represented groups?

options.text: To guarantee promotion for the members of the group
To widen access to opportunity, while selection still follows merit
To reduce the standard of entry for people in the group
To replace open competition for posts at that grade

questions.hint: Programmes widen access, not guarantee results.

items.title: L14: Succession planning versus open competition
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Civil Service talent guidance
items.body: Departments want to know who could fill key posts in future, so many run succession planning and talent management: identifying people with potential, giving them development and tracking their readiness. These are legitimate management activities, but they sit alongside, not above, the Recruitment Principles. Succession planning may inform development decisions, such as who gets a stretch assignment, and it may help a department see where gaps lie. It cannot be used to fill a post without competition. When a vacancy arises, it must be filled on merit after fair and open competition, unless an exception applies, and being on a talent list does not give a right to the post or to extra marks. A manager who says that a person is next in line is describing a hope, not a decision. Problems arise when talent decisions are made on narrow information, such as visibility to senior leaders, and when people who are not on a list receive fewer opportunities as a result. Good practice is to explain how people are identified, offer self-nomination, review decisions regularly, and ensure the criteria for talent spots mirror the Success Profiles for the future role. Individuals can ask how the department identifies talent, whether they are considered, and what they could do to be included. A department can lawfully run a talent scheme that gives development to chosen participants, provided it does not treat participation as a promotion and allows others to compete for posts on equal terms. Where a department treats a talent list as a closed pool, concerns can be raised through HR and, if needed, the Commission.

questions.prompt: What is succession planning?

options.text: Planning the removal of poor performers from key posts
Planning the retirement dates of all staff over a certain age
Appointing a named successor to each senior post without a competition
Identifying and developing people who could fill key posts in future

questions.hint: It is a development and workforce tool.

questions.prompt: Can a department fill a post straight from a talent list?

options.text: It can, if the line manager agrees in writing
It cannot, since posts need competition unless an exception applies
It can, if the person on the list is ranked first by managers
It can, if the post is urgent and the person is available

questions.hint: Talent lists do not replace competition.

questions.prompt: A manager says a person is next in line. What does this describe?

options.text: A hope, not a decision
An approved promotion that has not yet been announced
A legal entitlement to the post for the person named
A binding commitment that the department must honour

questions.prompt: What problem arises when talent decisions rest on visibility to senior leaders?

options.text: Senior leaders lose authority over who is appointed
The talent list becomes too large for HR to manage
People who are less visible receive fewer opportunities
It breaches data protection law in every circumstance

questions.prompt: Which feature makes a talent scheme fairer?

options.text: Explaining how people are identified and allowing self-nomination
Limiting the scheme to one department to keep it small
Allowing managers to add names whenever they wish
Keeping the criteria for selection confidential to avoid dispute

questions.prompt: How should criteria for talent spots be set?

options.text: By the manager's judgement alone, recorded in private
To mirror the Success Profiles for the future role
By the preferences of the most senior leader in the department
By length of service in the department up to that point

questions.hint: Criteria should relate to the role.

questions.prompt: What can an individual ask the department about talent management?

options.text: Who is on the list and what each person scored
Who will be promoted into each post next year
Whether the list can be changed in their favour
How it identifies talent and what you could do to be included

questions.hint: Ask about the process, not others' data.

questions.prompt: Is a talent scheme lawful if it gives development to chosen participants?

options.text: It is lawful only if participants are chosen by lot
It is lawful only if every member of staff takes part
It is, if participation is not treated as promotion
It is never lawful, because development must be open to everyone

questions.hint: Development is allowed; promotion needs competition.

questions.prompt: Where should concerns about a closed talent pool be raised?

options.text: Only through trade union officials in the department
Only through the minister's private office
Only through a public statement to the press
Through HR and, if needed, the Commission

questions.prompt: How do succession planning and the Principles relate?

options.text: They sit alongside each other, and succession planning cannot override the Principles
Succession planning replaces advertising for posts at the top
The Principles apply only to external recruitment, not internal
Succession planning overrides the Principles for senior posts

items.title: L14: When temporary promotion has run too long
items.source: Civil Service Recruitment Principles; departmental HR policy
items.body: Temporary promotion should be exactly that. Departments set maximum periods for temporary promotions, often around a year or two, and extensions normally need approval and a business case. A long-running arrangement that is repeatedly extended can become a way of filling a permanent need without competition, which is contrary to the Principles. Indicators that a temporary promotion has run too long include no end date, repeated extensions, the same person always selected, no plan to advertise the permanent post and other staff expressing concern. If you are the person acting up, ask for a date by which the post will be advertised, and accept that the right outcome may be a competition you may or may not win. Keep the evidence from your time in the role. If you are a manager, record the reason for each extension, consider whether the post should be advertised, and avoid giving the impression that the role belongs to the acting person. If you are a colleague who is concerned, you can raise it first with the line manager and then with HR or the nominated officer. A department can fix the problem by advertising the permanent post, which could be done as an internal competition if justified, and by setting an end date for the acting arrangement. In some cases, a role that has been done at a higher grade for a long time because duties have grown may be a case for job evaluation and regrading, which is a different process: it concerns the grade of the job, not who holds it. The two should not be confused, and a regrade does not create a right for the existing holder to be appointed to the regraded post without competition where the Principles apply.

questions.prompt: Which sign suggests temporary promotion has run too long?

options.text: A short extension of a few weeks to cover an absence
Two different people have each acted in the role for part of the time
Repeated extensions, no end date and no plan to advertise the permanent post
A clear review point after twelve months, with a plan to advertise

questions.prompt: What do departments usually need for an extension?

options.text: Nothing, since extensions are automatic once the post is vacant
Approval and a business case
The agreement of the acting person alone, since they are affected
A vote of the team members who work with the acting person

questions.prompt: You are acting up for a long time. What is a sensible request?

options.text: Ask for a date by which the permanent post will be advertised
Ask for the post to be given to you permanently without a competition
Ask for the acting arrangement to be made permanent by letter
Ask for your substantive grade to be raised in recognition

questions.prompt: As a manager, what should you do when extending a temporary promotion?

options.text: Extend without recording a reason, since the need is obvious
Tell the acting person that the job will be theirs in the end
Avoid telling HR in case the arrangement is questioned
Record the reason and consider whether the post should be advertised

questions.prompt: A colleague is concerned about a long acting arrangement. Whom can they first approach?

options.text: The press, which can draw attention to the situation
The minister's office, which will decide who gets the post
The line manager, then HR or the nominated officer
The panel of the permanent post, which will judge the acting person

questions.prompt: How can a department fix a long-running arrangement?

options.text: Appoint the acting person permanently without competition to end the issue
Advertise the permanent post and set an end date
Cancel the post so that the question no longer arises
Rotate the acting person to another post to hide the problem

questions.prompt: In Civil Service pay and grading, what is regrading?

options.text: Re-grading a job after evaluation because duties have grown
Promoting a person into a higher grade after an assessment
Moving a person to a lower grade at their own request
Changing a person's pay on the anniversary of their appointment

questions.hint: Regrading concerns the job, not the holder.

questions.prompt: Does regrading give the current holder a right to the regraded post?

options.text: It does if their manager agrees that they deserve it
It does, because they were doing the work before it was regraded
It does not where the Principles apply, as appointment still needs competition
It does if they ask in writing within a month

questions.prompt: Why must a regrade not be confused with temporary promotion?

options.text: A temporary promotion changes the grade of the job for ever
One concerns the grade of the job, the other who does a higher job for a time
They are the same process described under two different names
A regrade is always temporary, like an acting arrangement

questions.prompt: Which statement about extensions is most accurate?

options.text: Extensions are required after the first year of any arrangement

Extensions are approved automatically by the Commission each year

items.title: L14: Raising concerns about unfair recruitment
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998; Civil Service Commission
items.body: The Civil Service Code sets out the values of integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality, and it gives civil servants a route to raise concerns if they are asked to act in a way that conflicts with the Code or if they see wrongdoing. Unfair recruitment can fall within this: a post filled without advert, a panel member with an undeclared relationship, pressure to change scores or tailoring criteria to a person. A civil servant who has a concern should first raise it with their line manager or, if that is not appropriate, with a nominated officer or senior leader in the department. Departments have a nominated officer, and the Code says that civil servants will not be victimised for raising a concern in good faith. If the concern is not resolved, a civil servant can bring it to the Civil Service Commission, which considers complaints under the Code. There are also whistleblowing protections under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 for workers who make qualifying disclosures, usually where there is a belief, reasonably held, that there has been a breach of a legal obligation or other listed wrongdoing, and who make them in the manner the law provides. Before raising a concern, gather facts and keep notes, avoid speculation and avoid sharing the information more widely than necessary. Remember that a concern is about the process, not about someone's character. Do not take documents that you are not entitled to, and take advice on confidentiality and the Official Secrets Act where it applies. If you are on the receiving end of a concern, treat it seriously and fairly.

questions.prompt: Which route does the Civil Service Code give a civil servant who sees wrongdoing?

options.text: To make the concern public immediately through the press
To wait until the end of the year before saying anything
Raise it with a line manager, nominated officer or senior leader
To discuss it only with colleagues who are on the same grade

questions.prompt: What protection does the Code give a person who raises a concern in good faith?

options.text: They will be excused from the duties that gave rise to the concern
They will not be victimised for doing so
They will be promoted at the next opportunity as a reward
They will receive a pay rise in recognition of their honesty

questions.hint: The Code protects those who raise concerns.

questions.prompt: If a concern is not resolved internally, where can a civil servant take it?

options.text: To the head of another department, who can decide the matter
To a newspaper that has an interest in public bodies
To the next general election, through the minister
To the Civil Service Commission

questions.prompt: Which Act gives whistleblowing protections to workers who make qualifying disclosures?

options.text: The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
The Data Protection Act 2018, which deals with personal data
The Equality Act 2010, which deals with discrimination only
The Official Secrets Act 1989, which restricts disclosure

questions.prompt: Which action is a good first step before raising a concern?

options.text: Gather facts and keep notes without speculating
Share your suspicions widely to gain support from colleagues
Take documents you are not entitled to see so that you have proof
Confront the person you suspect and ask them to explain

questions.prompt: A concern should be about

options.text: The reputation of the manager concerned in the competition
The process and the facts rather than someone's character
The motives of each panel member as you imagine them

questions.prompt: Which example could fall within the Code concern route?

options.text: A disagreement about the scoring of a single answer
A personal dislike of a colleague who was successful
A delay of a few days in getting the results of a sift
A post filled without advert where the Principles required it

questions.hint: Unfair process can be a breach.

questions.prompt: Who is a nominated officer?

options.text: A trade union representative appointed for each department
A candidate chosen by the panel to speak for all applicants
A person designated in the department to receive concerns under the Code
The minister's private secretary, who handles correspondence

questions.prompt: Which behaviour would be inappropriate when raising a concern?

options.text: Taking documents you are not entitled to and sharing them

Keeping notes of what you saw and when it happened
Taking advice on confidentiality before you share information

questions.prompt: If someone raises a concern with you as a manager, what should you do?

options.text: Ask the person to withdraw it so that no formal process is needed

Tell the person that recruitment is not their business

items.title: L14: Counter-offers, retention and when to stay
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; departmental pay and HR policy
items.body: When you tell your department you have a promotion offer elsewhere, you may be asked to stay. Retention offers in the Civil Service are limited, and not every department can match a promotion, because pay and grade follow competition and pay policy. A manager may offer a stretch role, acting up, a development move, flexible working or a promise to look at your grade. Think carefully about each. Acting up or a stretch role may give evidence but is temporary and does not make you promoted. A promise to regrade your job is not a promise to promote you, because regrading follows job evaluation and the Principles still apply to who is appointed. A verbal assurance about a future promotion carries little weight because promotion is by competition. A market supplement for a shortage skill is possible in some departments, but is set by policy and not by personal negotiation. Before deciding, remind yourself why you applied: if you wanted a bigger role, a pay rise, a change of location or a new field, ask whether the counter-offer addresses it or just delays it. Consider the signal: a department that offers a better deal only when you are leaving may not value you in the normal way. Weigh the risk that your relationship with your manager changes after you have tried to leave, and the lost chance if you decline a good offer. If you accept the new post, do so cleanly and keep relationships positive, since you may work with the department again. If you stay, ask for any commitments in writing and review them after a defined period.

questions.prompt: Why can a department not always match a promotion offer?

options.text: Promotions are available only to external candidates in any competition
Departments are barred by law from keeping staff who have applied elsewhere
Pay and grade follow competition and pay policy
Managers never have any influence over grade or pay in the department

questions.prompt: What does a promise to regrade your job mean?

options.text: It guarantees the regraded post will be given to you
It guarantees you a pay rise in the next pay round
It is a promise to promote you into the regraded post
It does not promise promotion, as it concerns the job

questions.prompt: Why does a verbal assurance of future promotion carry little weight?

options.text: Verbal assurances are always untrue when they concern careers
Managers are not allowed to discuss careers with staff
Promotion is by fair and open competition, so no one can promise it
Written assurances are not permitted under HR policy

questions.prompt: How is a market supplement for a shortage skill usually set?

options.text: By the candidate's former pay at the previous post
By the individual's own request, supported by a job offer elsewhere
By the manager's discretion alone, recorded in an email
By departmental policy rather than personal negotiation

questions.prompt: Which question should you ask before deciding on a counter-offer?

options.text: Whether it addresses why you applied or merely delays the issue
Whether the new post has better parking than the current building
Whether the panel who interviewed you will remember you
Whether your manager will be annoyed if you say yes to the offer

questions.hint: Match the offer to your motivation.

questions.prompt: What might it signal when a better deal appears only when you are leaving?

options.text: That the department has no budget to keep people at all
The department may not value staff in the normal course of business
That the department is generous in all cases to its staff
That the department wants you to leave for good

questions.prompt: Which risk follows trying to leave and then staying?

options.text: You cannot apply for any other post for twelve months
Your continuous service in the department is lost
Your grade is reduced as a mark of disloyalty
Your relationship with your manager may change

questions.prompt: If you accept the new post, what is good practice?

options.text: Take confidential information with you for future reference
Do so cleanly and keep relationships positive
Delay telling your manager until the last moment so that the offer is secure
Criticise the department's culture on your way out

questions.prompt: If you decide to stay after a counter-offer, what should you do?

options.text: Ask for commitments in writing and review them after a defined period
Tell colleagues about the offer so that they know your worth
Apply again straight away for another post elsewhere
Rely on the verbal promises made at the meeting

questions.prompt: Which counter-offer gives the most useful evidence for a later promotion?

options.text: A supplement for loyalty that is not linked to the role
A promise to think about your grade at some point
A stretch role or acting up that provides higher-grade evidence

questions.hint: Evidence helps, though it is temporary.

items.title: L14: Making a strong complaint to the Commission
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Commission complaints guidance
items.body: A complaint to the Civil Service Commission about recruitment is a formal step, and it works best when it is well prepared. First, the Commission normally expects the department's own complaints process to have been completed, so you need the department's final response. The complaint should then identify the specific Recruitment Principle you believe was breached, such as selection on merit through fair and open competition, and the facts that support it. State what happened, when and who was involved, enclose relevant documents such as the advert, correspondence and the department's response, and describe the outcome you seek. Keep to facts and avoid personal attacks or speculation, because the Commission is looking at the process and not at personal feelings. There is a time limit for bringing a complaint, so act promptly after the department's response. The Commission examines whether the Principles were breached and may ask the department for its records and an explanation. It does not re-score candidates, determine who is better for the post or overturn individual appointments as a general rule; it can find that the Principles were not followed and recommend what the department should do, which may include changes to its processes. A finding may not change your own result, but it can improve practice. Some matters fall outside its remit, for example employment tribunal claims for discrimination, which have separate routes and time limits, so consider the right forum for each element. Expect the process to take time, and keep copies of everything.

questions.prompt: What does the Commission normally expect before it will consider a recruitment complaint?

options.text: That you have made a public statement about the competition
That you have spoken to the panel chair about the outcome
That the department's own complaints process has been completed

questions.prompt: What should a complaint identify?

options.text: The Principle believed breached and the supporting facts

questions.prompt: Which documents are useful to enclose?

options.text: Your own appraisals over the past five years

options.text: Brief, with no detail, so that the facts speak for themselves

Forceful, so that the complaint gains attention at once
Emotional, so that the impact on you is clear to the reader

options.text: Whether the panel liked the candidate who complained

Whether the Principles were breached
Whether the department should pay compensation to the candidate

options.text: It does so whenever the complainant asks it to
It does so whenever a complaint is upheld by its staff

options.text: It entitles you to damages from the department

questions.prompt: Which matter would fall outside the Commission's remit?

options.text: An employment tribunal claim for discrimination

options.text: The panel may change its mind about the outcome

options.text: Only the final decision letter, since it contains everything

Copies of everything you send and receive

items.title: L14: Planning a three-year route to Grade 7
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Behaviours
items.body: A realistic route from SEO or HEO to Grade 7 takes planning, not just ambition. Begin with the Grade 7 Success Profile: behaviours at the fourth level, relevant experience and any technical or professional requirements. Compare your current evidence honestly and write a gap list. Plan the three years in stages. In the first year, close the biggest gaps: take on work that involves leading others, managing a budget or influencing senior stakeholders, and ask for feedback from someone who can compare you with Grade 7 colleagues. In the second year, extend scope by acting up, taking a loan, or leading a cross-team project, and begin to apply for a few Grade 7 posts to test the market and gather feedback, accepting that early attempts may not succeed. In the third year, apply for posts that match your evidence, refine your examples from feedback and keep your profile visible. Build support: a line manager who knows your plan, a mentor, and a sponsor at Grade 7 or above. Consider the choice of profession, as some professions have clearer pathways to Grade 7 than others, and some departments recruit more at Grade 7 than others. Review your plan every six months and adjust for changes in vacancies, circumstances and feedback. Be prepared for a move of department or location if the best opportunity requires it. Balance the plan with wellbeing and the demands of your life outside work. The plan does not guarantee promotion, because posts are filled by competition, but it increases the chance that your evidence is strong when a suitable post appears.

options.text: The date on which you would like to be promoted
